title: Hinduism: the lamp and the flower
hookLine: daily worship at home often begins with a lamp and a flower

lines: A SMALL SHRINE IN THE KITCHEN.
cards: Early morning in millions of Hindu homes, before the kettle, before the school run.
In a corner of the kitchen, a small cabinet, or a shelf in the living room, there's a little shrine: an image of a god, maybe Ganesha or Krishna or the goddess Lakshmi.
Someone, often a grandmother or a mother, strikes a match, lights a small lamp, and sets down a fresh flower. Maybe a bell rings once. Maybe it takes two minutes.
Then the day begins. This is puja.

teach.b: Puja is the Sanskrit word for worship, honor, reverent attention. It can be grand, in a temple with priests, drums and hundreds of people, or tiny, one person at a home shrine before work. At its heart it's hospitality.
The god is welcomed like an honored guest, and offered what you'd offer a guest: light, water, fragrance, flowers, food.
The image in the shrine is called a murti, and many Hindus understand the deity as truly present in it during worship. A guest's note: murti is a better word than idol, which carries old insults.
The lamp is often the first offering: a small clay or brass lamp, a diya, burning ghee or oil.
In a ritual called aarti, the flame is waved in slow circles before the murti, then carried around, and people pass their hands over it and draw the warmth to their eyes and head.
The food offered is afterward shared as prasad, a blessed gift. There's also darshan, which means seeing: to see the god, and to be seen. And the flower?

teach.h: A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.
teach.b: In the Bhagavad Gita, chapter nine, verse twenty-six, Krishna says that whoever offers him with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, he accepts it.
The size of the gift doesn't matter; the love in it does. Hindu homes differ hugely: different gods, different families, different rules, and many Hindus don't keep a daily puja at all.
But the shape of it is simple and very human: begin the day by offering light.

how: Many Hindu households keep a home shrine and perform a short daily puja: lighting a lamp and incense, offering flowers, water or food to the murti, sometimes with aarti and a prayer, before the day begins.

o: a day of fasting kept in honor of a favorite god
a barefoot pilgrimage to a faraway mountain shrine
worship that welcomes a god as an honored guest

p: the sacred image in the shrine
offered food, shared as a gift
to see the god, and be seen

s: it can be grand in a temple or tiny at a home shrine before work.
the Gita says a leaf or a flower offered with devotion is accepted
Krishna says a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, offered with love (Gita 9.26).
every Hindu family does puja the same way
different gods, different families, different rules; many don't keep a daily puja.

games.q: you're a guest in a Hindu home during evening aarti. the lamp is brought around to you. what do you do?
o: pass your hands over the flame and draw them toward your face, if you're comfortable.
games.why: during aarti, people pass their hands over the flame and draw the warmth to their eyes and head. guests are usually welcome to join or simply to watch.

practice: If you have a candle and it's safe, light it now, and set a flower, a leaf or even a glass of water beside it; if not, picture a small lamp in a quiet corner. Watch the flame.
Let this be a small act of attention: something offered, not asked for.

wordCard.voice: Puja. Hindu worship, often at a home shrine: light, water, flowers and food offered to the god as to an honored guest. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Hindi: worship, honor, reverent attention.

carryVoice: Your line: one flame. A leaf or a flower, given with love, is plenty. Day two hundred thirty-seven.
